Keyword search (TF-IDF) scores a movie by the words its plot summary shares with your question. Embedding search turns your question and each plot summary into a list of numbers, then ranks the movies whose numbers are closest to your question's.

First prediction: **for questions that name a character, place or thing, which method will do better, and why?** A sentence or two is enough, and a guess is fine.

TF-IDF because it looks at plot summary in correspondence with a question, so instead of finding ranks of words, it will better isolate parts of the document that carries an answer close to the character, place, or thing.

**Part 1: Build the TF-IDF model (about 6 minutes)**

Most people get through Part 3 or 4 in class. Whatever is left, including Part 5, is due 8:00am Thursday, October 22.

`tfidf_settings.py` has three settings:

1. **`REMOVE_STOP_WORDS`** (True or False; now **False**). When True, it drops about 300 common words before scoring. Take "The dog ran to the store": with True, only "dog ran store" is left. The list is scikit-learn's, and it goes further than "the" and "of". It also drops words like "bill", "fire", "name" and "system", and the number words "one" through "twelve", except "seven".

2. **`MIN_MOVIES`** (a whole number, 1 or more; now **1**). It keeps only the words that appear in at least that many plot summaries. Say "Gondor" appears in just one summary. Then 1 keeps it, and 2 or more drops it. 1 is the only value that keeps a word found in a single summary.

3. **`REPEATS_COUNT_LESS`** (True or False; now **False**). When True, a word that repeats within one summary counts as 1 + log(count) instead of its raw count. So "shark" appearing 4 times counts as about 2.4 instead of 4.

Words are always lowercased, so "Dog" and "dog" are one word. That isn't a setting.

What value do you choose for each of the three, and why? Give a reason for each, all in one reply. A sentence apiece is enough.

**User:**
1. Drop about 300 common words. 2. Keep summaries that share at least one common word. 3. True

**What a sentence embedding is.** On October 1 you saw GloVe, which gives each word a list of numbers. Words used in similar contexts get similar lists, so "film" and "movie" land close together. A sentence model does the same thing for a whole sentence or plot summary. It turns the full text into one list of numbers (here, 384 of them). Two texts that mean similar things get lists that are close, even if they share few exact words. Search ranks the movies whose summary's list is closest to your question's list.

Here are your two Part 0 predictions, as you wrote them:

> **Questions that name a character, place or thing:** TF-IDF because it looks at plot summary in correspondence with a question, so instead of finding ranks of words, it will better isolate parts of the document that carries an answer close to the character, place, or thing.

> **Vague descriptions:** Embeddings will do better because it isn't looking for words that are rare or special, it is looking into words that are related. Vague questions will lead to vague answers, but at least they will be on topic.
